drills.q: Define G, M, and P precisely, and state what actually bounds truly parallel Go-code execution at any instant.
drills.a: G=goroutine (lightweight user-space unit of work), M=OS thread (kernel-scheduled), P=logical processor context, exactly GOMAXPROCS of them, each with a local run queue up to 256 entries. An M must hold a P to execute Go code, so the P count bounds parallel execution -- not the M count, since M count can temporarily exceed GOMAXPROCS when a P detaches from a blocked M and reattaches to another.

drills.q: Explain Go's goroutine stack growth mechanism and why the same technique isn't safely available to a naive C runtime.
drills.a: A goroutine's stack starts at 2KB; a cheap check at function entry detects insufficient room and triggers allocating a larger stack, copying the old contents over, and rewriting every pointer in the copied data that referenced the old stack's address range to point into the new stack. This is safe only because the Go compiler emits precise stack maps telling the runtime exactly which stack words are pointers versus plain data -- a C runtime generally can't distinguish a genuine pointer from an integer that merely looks like one, so blind pointer rewriting isn't safely possible there.

drills.q: What changed in Go 1.14's scheduler, what specific bug class did it fix, and what should you suspect if apparent goroutine starvation appears on a modern Go version?
drills.a: Go 1.14 introduced asynchronous preemption via OS signals, interrupting a running goroutine at arbitrary points instead of only at function-call safe points, fixing the pre-1.14 bug where a tight loop with no calls could starve peer goroutines on the same P indefinitely. On 1.14+, that specific cause is ruled out by version -- suspect instead a goroutine holding a lock/resource for a pathologically long time, or a GOMAXPROCS misconfiguration relative to actual available CPU.

drills.q: A Go service in a Kubernetes pod with a 2-core CPU limit shows scheduling throttling despite low reported CPU usage. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Pre-Go-1.25, GOMAXPROCS defaults to the host's total core count, not the container's cgroup CPU limit, so the scheduler oversubscribes Ps relative to the actual CPU quota, triggering cgroup CFS throttling. Fix: upgrade to Go 1.25+ (container-aware GOMAXPROCS by default) or explicitly set GOMAXPROCS to the container's limit (or use uber-go/automaxprocs on older versions).

drills.q: Explain V8 hidden classes and why two objects with identical final property sets can still have different hidden classes.
drills.a: A hidden class (V8's Map) encodes an object's property set and storage offsets, determined by the TRANSITION HISTORY of property additions, not just the final set. Two objects with the same final properties but added in different orders (e.g. x-then-y vs y-then-x) end up with two distinct hidden classes despite looking identical from JS code, defeating the fast fixed-offset access path -- consistent construction order (ideally via one shared constructor/factory) is what actually matters for performance.

drills.q: Distinguish monomorphic, polymorphic, and megamorphic inline caches, and explain what happens to TurboFan's optimization once a site goes megamorphic.
drills.a: Monomorphic: one hidden class ever observed at the site, fastest case (single cached fixed-offset access, no branching). Polymorphic: a small bounded number of distinct shapes (commonly up to ~4), still reasonably fast via a small dispatch table. Megamorphic: more shapes than the polymorphic cache holds, fast path abandoned entirely, falling back to generic slow property lookup -- and TurboFan, seeing megamorphic feedback, declines to generate type-specialized code for that site since there's no stable shape to speculate on.

drills.q: A Node.js function that was previously fast slows down sharply under production load with no code change. Walk through the diagnostic process.
drills.a: Suspect a deoptimization or a shift from monomorphic/polymorphic to megamorphic inline caches at a hot property-access site, likely triggered by a change in the DATA flowing through the function (a new upstream source producing objects with different property-addition order, or values shifting from consistently-integer to sometimes-float) rather than a code change. Diagnose with --trace-deopt (specific deopt events/reasons/locations) and --trace-ic (IC state transitions), and rule out GC pressure changes in parallel via --trace-gc rather than guessing which cause applies.

drills.q: Explain deoptimization in V8 and how it's architecturally similar to mechanisms in other runtimes.
drills.a: When TurboFan-compiled machine code's speculative assumption (a stable hidden class, or a value always being an integer) is violated at runtime, V8 discards the optimized code, reconstructs an equivalent interpreter-level stack frame, and resumes execution in Ignition. This is the same 'speculate aggressively, keep a safe correct fallback' pattern as the JVM's C2 deoptimization back to the interpreter and CPython's 3.11+ specializing adaptive interpreter de-specializing a bytecode site when its type guard fails.

drills.q: Staff-level: your team is deciding between unbounded per-request goroutines and a fixed worker pool for a high-throughput ingestion service. Make the case for each and give a recommendation.
drills.a: Unbounded per-request goroutines are simplest and fine as long as incoming rate times average goroutine lifetime stays within what downstream resources (DB connections, memory, file descriptors) and process memory can sustain -- goroutines being cheap doesn't make downstream dependencies infinitely scalable. A bounded worker pool or semaphore trades minor code complexity for a hard, predictable concurrency ceiling and natural backpressure, protecting downstream resources under traffic spikes. Recommendation: for a high-throughput ingestion service specifically, a bounded pool/limiter is the safer default, sized generously relative to measured downstream capacity rather than arbitrarily small -- unbounded goroutines under a spike (memory exhaustion, downstream connection exhaustion) is a real, common production incident pattern.

drills.q: Why is spawning 100,000 goroutines routine in Go while spawning 100,000 OS threads is impractical? Give the concrete memory math.
drills.a: Goroutine stacks start at 2KB and grow on demand, versus an OS thread's typical fixed default of 1-8MB reserved upfront. 100,000 goroutines at 2KB each is roughly 200MB total; 100,000 OS threads at even a conservative 2MB each is roughly 200GB -- an infeasible memory footprint, plus each OS thread carries real kernel-level context-switch and scheduling cost that goroutines' user-space scheduling avoids.
